frame: Busking music drifts across the harbour. The Whoshell wants to know who wrote this story.
text: Vic has played me every Saturday morning outside the Twotide bakery since 1971. I have a dent from the time he dropped me off the ferry, and a second dent from the time he sat on me at a wedding. My valves stick in cold weather, and I sound, as Vic likes to say, 'like a walrus with a head cold'. Last Saturday, though, Vic's hands were too sore to play. He sat on the bench with his thermos while his granddaughter, Mei, lifted me out of the case. She had never played a tuba before. She was nine years old and not much taller than I am. 'I'll just try one note,' she said. She took an enormous breath, pressed her lips to my mouthpiece and blew so hard that a pigeon took off from the bakery roof in fright. It was not a good note. It was, however, extremely loud, and the crowd that had been ignoring us for fifty years suddenly turned to look. Mei blew again, and then again, until the notes began to wobble into something like a tune. By lunchtime, Vic's hat was full of coins. Mei has decided she will play me every Saturday from now on, and I have decided to let her.

text: Tom played the triangle in the Twotide school band, right at the back, behind the tubas. At the start of every song, he counted carefully and waited for his moment. Ting. And still, nobody heard Tom. The trumpets were loud, the drums were louder, and the tubas sounded like a herd of cows having an argument. At the spring concert, Tom polished his triangle until it gleamed. He hit it as hard as he dared. Ting. And still, nobody heard Tom. His mum clapped for the drummer by mistake. frame: The Murkle hitched a ride on a whale-watching boat. It found this log in a bunk.
text: Whale-watching log, Saturday. We left the harbour at seven, and by nine the skipper, Dee, had spotted a humpback mother and her calf about two hundred metres off the bow. I watched them through the binoculars for nearly an hour: the mother rolling lazily on the surface, the calf slapping its tail again and again as if it were practising. My cousin Rafi had gone out on the smaller research boat that morning, and over the radio he told us that his team had dropped an underwater microphone and recorded the mother singing. I would have given anything to hear it, but the radio was too crackly to play it back. Just before lunch, the pair dived and didn't come up again. Dee told us humpbacks can stay under for up to forty-five minutes, so we waited, eating soggy sandwiches and staring at the empty sea. A seagull stole half of mine. They never came back up where we could see them. We headed back to the harbour at three, sunburnt and quiet. Rafi says the recording is too precious to email, so I won't hear it until he gets home next month. Tonight, in my bunk, I keep wondering where the calf is now.

text: When we went away for the long weekend, Dad left our robot vacuum, Dusty, switched on to 'patrol mode', which he said would keep the house clean while we were gone. On Saturday, Dad and I checked the app on his phone. The little map showed Dusty's path as a neat blue line zigzagging around the lounge room. On Sunday morning, the blue line went through the dog flap, across the back lawn and under the side fence. Dad and I watched the live camera on Dusty's lid as it showed grass, then a garden gnome, then the inside of Mrs Agosti's chook shed. Dad went very quiet. Then he laughed so hard that he had to sit down on the sand. We were three hours away at the beach, so nobody could go and get it. We tried calling Mrs Agosti, but she was away too. When we finally got home on Monday night, Dusty was sitting in our driveway, fully charged, with a feather stuck to its brush and an egg balanced on its lid. Our dog sniffed it suspiciously. The camera had switched off at lunchtime on Sunday, so to this day nobody knows how it got home.

frame: Narra the Teller tells this tale only to visitors who stay until sunset.
text: Every autumn, the shearwater chicks of Twotide Atoll leave their burrows and fly north, thousands of kilometres across open ocean, without a single adult to show them the way. Kip was the last chick left on the island. Each evening he waddled to the top of the dune, spread his wings, stared at the endless grey water and waddled straight back down his burrow. His feathers were ready. His wings were strong. It was the rest of him that wasn't. The other chicks had left weeks earlier, and his parents had gone too, as shearwater parents always do, so the burrow grew colder and Kip grew hungrier. Then, one evening, a storm rolled in, and the waves began to eat away at the dune, metre by metre, until the sea was lapping at the mouth of his burrow. Kip had always thought of the burrow as the safe place and the sky as the dangerous one. Now, for the first time, staying was more frightening than going. He scrambled to the top of the last patch of sand, shut his eyes and jumped into the wind. He didn't fly well. He wobbled, dipped and nearly clipped a wave. But he flew. By the time the sun came up, the island was a speck behind him, and Kip was no longer afraid of the sky. He was far too busy looking for breakfast.
